title: Candidates Hit Crunch Time With One Week Until Election Day
summary:
With Election Day just over a week away, candidates across the United States are in crunch time. Control of Congress is at stake in the midterm elections, and the biggest names in both parties hit the campaign trail this weekend.

On Monday, President Donald Trump campaigned in Mississippi, a state he won by almost 23 points two years ago. Over the weekend, the battleground state of Michigan hosted a political heavyweight bout between Trump and former President Barack Obama.

In Michigan, a tight Senate race will help decide which party controls the Senate. The contest pits former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who would be the nation's first Muslim senator. Trump attacked El-Sayed's faith and said he would be a threat to national security. El-Sayed answered that the attacks were a distraction from voters' concerns about the economy. Rogers, in an interview on NBC's 'Meet the Press,' stood by his claims linking El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, even though there is no evidence El-Sayed has any affiliation with the group.

Obama rallied Democratic voters in Michigan and Ohio on Saturday, telling crowds that Trump was responsible for rising costs because of the war with Iran. He said the current president chose to start an unnecessary war that nobody voted for. Obama also poked fun at Trump's focus on his Washington, D.C., renovation projects, joking about all the gold.

Voters waiting in line at the rallies spoke about what will draw them to the polls. One Michigan resident said he was there for the future of the country, because the nation is at a crossroads.

Late Monday, in a separate development, a federal appeals court denied a Justice Department request to block California from counting some 20,000 mail-in ballots from voters it alleges are potential non-citizens.
why_it_matters: The midterm elections will decide which party controls Congress, and that shapes the laws that affect people's daily lives, including the economy voters are worried about.

A state where the result is close and either party could win.
The trips and rallies candidates make to win votes.

A court that reviews decisions made by lower courts.

background_read: A midterm election is an election held partway through a president's time in office, when control of Congress is at stake.
Congress is the law-making body, and the Senate is one of its two parts; a Senate race can help decide which party controls it.
Candidates travel to campaign in states where races are tight, holding rallies to win over voters.
Mail-in ballots are votes sent by mail rather than cast in person, and courts can be asked to decide whether they should be counted.
